archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: An undrafted rookie backup whose most reliable offense came from pulling the ball down and running, while his passing stayed short, safe in design and shaky in execution.

report.headline: His legs kept him afloat; his passing rarely reached the sticks.
report.take:
Jalon Daniels is Tampa Bay's QB2. He took over for Baker Mayfield for three starts in Weeks 4-6, went 1-2, and handed the job back when Mayfield returned in Week 7. His season is essentially those three games plus mop-up snaps, 98 attempts in all, so read everything here as a scouting report on a spot starter rather than a settled profile. He has no career history to check it against.

The running is the part that worked. He scrambled on 13% of his dropbacks, and those 16 scrambles produced 119 yards and 7 first downs at +0.451 EPA per scramble. His rushing EPA was positive in every start, and he ranks 10th among qualifiers in rushing yards per game. The passing told a different story. His intended air yards of 5.23 put the average throw more than four yards short of the sticks (airYdsToSticks -4.15), and he still ranks 46th of 49 in yards per attempt and adjusted net yards per dropback. Tampa Bay ran a conservative script around him: the offense sits 29th in pass rate over expected and leans on a defense ranked 2nd in EPA. Even with that cover, his dropbacks came out at -0.193 EPA, 41st in the league.

The splits show where it broke. Throws of 10-19 air yards were a disaster: 26.3% completions, -29 CPOE, 2 interceptions and -8.7 EPA on just 19 attempts. In close fourth quarters he completed 40.9% with three of his five picks, -14.7 EPA on 24 plays. His 18.4% bad-throw rate ranks 40th of 42. His connection with Emeka Egbuka, his most-targeted receiver, cost -15.3 EPA on 29 targets, while Cade Otton and Ted Hurst III were positive. That points to the hard, contested throws to his top option going wrong, not the whole passing game. The deep and red-zone numbers look good, at +1.036 EPA on 9 deep throws and 3 TDs on 9 red-zone attempts, but those are handfuls of plays and shouldn't move the evaluation.

The Week 6 loss to Pittsburgh dominates the season. That game produced 43 attempts, 5 sacks, a 26.8% bad-throw rate and -21.8 passing EPA, which is more than his entire season total. Against Dallas, now the 31st-ranked defense, he was clean and efficient (+5.9). Against good defenses asked to throw, he wasn't. That fits a backup who can manage a lead with his legs but can't yet carry a passing game.

strengths.title: Scrambling creates real value
strengths.body: When the first read isn't there, he pulls the ball down and runs, and it has paid. He turned 16 scrambles into 7 first downs at +0.45 EPA each, and his rushing EPA was positive in all three starts. It's the most repeatable part of his game because it doesn't depend on reading coverage or accuracy, and it would carry over into any future start.

strengths.title: No fumbles, solid under center
strengths.body: He hasn't lost a fumble despite the scrambling. He was also efficient on the few under-center, play-action-type snaps: 81.8% completions and positive EPA on 12 plays, against -0.221 EPA from shotgun. It's a small sample, but it suggests what a coordinator would build for him as a spot starter: a run-first, under-center plan with defined throws.

concerns.title: Intermediate throws are broken
concerns.body: The 10-19 yard window is where NFL starters earn first downs. He hit 26.3% there, 29 points below expectation, with two interceptions. Combined with throws that land well short of the sticks, defenses can squat underneath and dare him to fit the ball in. This is an accuracy and processing issue rather than a scheme artifact, and it is the main thing separating him from starter-level play.

concerns.title: Wilts when games tighten late
concerns.body: Within one score he was at -0.254 EPA per play with all five of his interceptions. In close fourth quarters it got worse: 40.9% completions and three picks. Some of that is the Pittsburgh game, where Tampa Bay had to throw 43 times, but it shows what happens when the run-first cover is removed and he has to win from the pocket.

concerns.title: Sacks and wild throws under duress
concerns.body: A third of his pressures became sacks, and his 8.4% sack rate is above the league average. Part of that is the cost of a scrambler hunting for running lanes, and his scrambles mostly pay it back. The bad-throw rate is not part of that trade. It ranks near the bottom and spiked to 26.8% against Pittsburgh.

trend.note: His starts swung from a turnover-marred loss to Green Bay, to a clean, efficient win over a bottom defense in Dallas, to a -21.8 EPA collapse against Pittsburgh. He has played only cameo snaps since Mayfield returned. His 'last 3' window includes one of those relief appearances, so it says little about current form.

nextGame.headline: Soft Detroit pass defense, but he's holding a clipboard
nextGame.body:
On paper Detroit is a defense he'd want to face. It allows the most fantasy points to quarterbacks, ranks 27th in pass EPA allowed, and is 28th against short throws, which is exactly where his game lives. The catch is pressure: the Lions rank 5th in hit rate and 7th in sack rate, and he turns pressure into sacks at a high clip. Detroit's offense is also 4th in pass EPA, so a game in which Tampa Bay has to keep pace through the air is the script that has hurt him most.

Availability is the whole question, and it starts with Mayfield, who started the last three games and carries no injury note. Daniels is listed as QB2, so barring an in-game injury he won't see meaningful snaps. Detroit's defense is depleted: corner D.J. Reed (94% of snaps) and safety Kerby Joseph were out as of Nov. 7-9, and linebacker Jack Campbell (97%) is on injured reserve. Reed's and Joseph's listed return dates are estimates that fall before this game, so their status is uncertain. Those absences help whoever plays quarterback for Tampa Bay. The game is in a dome, so weather is not a factor.

keyMatchups.title: Detroit's pass rush vs his sack habit
keyMatchups.body: Detroit gets home on passers more often than most, and he took a sack on a third of his pressured dropbacks. If he plays, his scrambling has to beat that rush, not feed it.

keyMatchups.title: Short-area throws vs a leaky underneath
keyMatchups.body: Detroit gives up positive EPA on short passes, and nearly three-quarters of his attempts were under 10 air yards. For a quarterback who can't yet attack the intermediate window, this is the matchup that would let a conservative plan function.

keyMatchups.title: Shootout script risk
keyMatchups.body: Detroit's offense is near the top of the league through the air. A game where Tampa Bay has to throw to keep up removes the run-heavy shell that protected him in his starts.

nextGame.watch: Whether Mayfield stays healthy; Daniels matters only if he's pressed into action.

restOfSeason.body:
As long as Mayfield is healthy, expect Daniels to show up only in relief or blowout snaps, with production near zero: think 0-25 passing yards and single-digit rushing in a typical week. If he's thrust back into the lineup, his starts suggest a floor-heavy line of roughly 140-190 passing yards and 25-45 rushing yards. He would likely play inside a run-first plan built to lean on Tampa Bay's 2nd-ranked defense. His rushing value is the sustainable part. The red-zone touchdowns and the deep-ball efficiency come from too few plays to count on.

Some regression should run in his favor. An interception rate over 5% on this volume is partly bad luck, and his intermediate accuracy is unlikely to stay quite this poor. But the low bad-throw ranking and the short, safe aim are traits, not noise. Any improvement would come from reps and a scheme that keeps him under center and on schedule.
swingFactors: A run-first, under-center game plan if he starts

confidence.note: 98 attempts over three starts, no career history, and a backup role that limits future snaps.
